query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Using electrospark deposition (ESPD) with a finer feedstock powder size can overcome the thickness shortfall of the FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.intervention: Electrospark deposition (ESPD) with a finer feedstock powder size
generation.conditions: Thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system
generation.mechanism: Reduced oxidation and improved coating density due to finer powder size and localized heating
generation.predicted_outcome: Increased coating thickness and improved coating integrity
generation.boundary: Thermal barrier coating system operating conditions
generation.uncertainty: Optimal feedstock powder size and ESPD process parameters for achieving desired coating thickness and integrity

falsification_experiment.design: Comparative study of FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coats deposited using ESPD with different feedstock powder sizes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coating thickness and integrity of the ESPD-deposited bond coat with a finer feedstock powder size are not significantly improved compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Therefore, in order to investigate the high-temperature protective capabilities of EHEA coatings, AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and AlCoCrFeNi2.1 co-doping with Y and Hf (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding in this paper. After their preparation, the microstructure and high-temperature thermal stability of the coatings were characterized, and the hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% (wt.%) NaCl mixed molten salt was investigated, which provided data support for an evaluation of the potential applications of high-entropy alloy coatings in harsh service environments such as steam pipelines and the hot-end components of gas turbines.

One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. In a gas-atomized state, the powder consisted of BCC supersaturated solid solution. The high rate of heating and cooling and high oxygen concentration during spraying led to oxidation development prior to decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution. Depleted Al layers of BCC transferred to the FCC phase. Zhao et al.  used a NiCrSiB powder-covered electrode to deposit metal matrix composites (MMC). Recently, electrospark was adopted for alloying Ti-Ni-Zr-Mo-Al-C composite coating on Ti-6Al-4 V surface for higher resistance to wear and high-temperature gas corrosion using metal/alloy powders Ti, Ni, Zr, Mo, Al and Ti3Al + 10%C mixture. These investigations suggest that powders can be one of the feedstocks in coating fabrication, and the “straightforward” combination of M/HEA coatings can be fabricated with ESPD, which could largely simplify the coating process and is readily for new alloy development, yet there is no study related to this approach. In addition to this manufacturing process, the ESPD can rapidly fabricate the M/HEA coating using conventional metal or alloy powder, which can largely reduce the cost, it can neglect the complex surface morphology of the substrate, and it has low requirements to the feedstock in terms of size and shape. The ESPD technique generally exhibits a lower deposition rate compared to other coating methods, making it more suitable for thin coatings.
